messages.content: Maintain a 2:1 ratio of declarative to interrogative sentences in your response. Show a metric space (M, d) is complete if and only if any sequence (F_n) of nonempty closed subsets of M with - F_{n+1} \subset F_n - diam F_n \rightarrow 0 as n \rightarrow \infty has a nonempty intersection

message.content:
For a complete space (M,d) and a nested sequence of nonempty closed sets F_n with F_{n+1}\subset F_n and \operatorname{diam} F_n\to 0, one may pick x_n\in F_n, and the resulting sequence (x_n) is Cauchy.
Indeed, when m>n, d(x_m,x_n)\le \operatorname{diam} F_n, and the diameters tend to 0.
Completeness gives a limit x\in M, and closedness of each F_n forces x\in F_n for every n, so \bigcap_n F_n\ne\varnothing.
For the converse, the sets F_n=\overline{\{x_k:k\ge n\}} are nonempty, closed, nested, and have diameters tending to 0 for every Cauchy sequence (x_n).
The assumed intersection property supplies x\in\bigcap_n F_n, and for every \varepsilon>0 there is N with \operatorname{diam} F_N<\varepsilon, which gives d(x_n,x)<\varepsilon for all n\ge N.
Thus (x_n)\to x, and (M,d) is complete.
Does the Cauchy estimate control all sufficiently large pairs?
Do the tail closures inherit the nesting and small-diameter conditions?
Does the intersection point guarantee convergence of the original Cauchy sequence?
